title: The search engine that doesn't snitch
pitch: A search engine over a company's internal documents that answers in plain language and cites which file it pulled each fact from. And when the intern asks about leadership salaries, it says it can't find anything, because for them that document doesn't exist.
outcome: A project that runs on your computer against a real database in the cloud. You type a question and an email, and it returns the answer with numbered sources and each one's similarity percentage. You swap the email for someone else's, ask the same question, and the answer changes because their permissions are different. That last part is what you show off in an interview: almost nobody has it.
time: 3-4 hours the first time, counting the fight with the connection string
requires: Python 3.10 or higher installed and working from the terminal (check with python --version).

A Supabase account with a project created, Central EU (Frankfurt) region. The Free plan is more than enough: €0, no card. Warning: if you don't touch the project for 7 days it pauses itself and you have to wake it up by hand from the dashboard.

That project's connection string (Project Settings > Database > Connection string > URI) and its password. If you lost the password you can set a new one right there, but the original can't be recovered.

An OpenAI API key. There's no free plan here: you need to load balance, minimum $5 (about €4.60). That's plenty: indexing these three documents costs less than a cent and each question costs about 3 thousandths of a cent.
Having used the terminal before. Knowing how to enter a folder with cd and run a file is enough.

structure.what: The list of libraries to install. Lets someone else set up the project in two minutes with a single command.
The key template, with names but no values. This one gets shared; the real one (.env) never leaves your computer.
The three tables, the search index, and the test people. Pasted into Supabase once.
The only place in the project that knows how to open the database. If you switch servers tomorrow, you touch this file and that's it.
Splits a long document into ~200-word chunks with overlap, so no sentence gets lost right at the cut.
Walks the docs/ folder, chunks each file, turns it into vectors, and saves it. Run every time the documents change.
Retrieves the 5 chunks most similar to a question, already filtered by the asker's permissions. This is the heart of the project.
The program you actually use. You give it an email and a question, and it returns the answer with numbered sources.

steps.title: Set up the folder, the libraries, and the sample documents
steps.why: Before writing a line of logic you need somewhere for it to live. Here you set up the structure and, above all, decide that the folder a document sits in is what determines who can read it. That decision saves you half an hour of headaches later. You also keep the key out of the code from minute one: in .env, which never gets pushed anywhere.
steps.code:
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The project folder.
#    Each subfolder of docs/ is an AREA: the folder name decides
#    who can read what's inside it. No exceptions.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
mkdir -p buscador-docs/docs/general buscador-docs/docs/finanzas buscador-docs/docs/direccion
cd buscador-docs

# 2. Virtual environment: a box of libraries only this project uses,
#    so it doesn't clutter your computer's Python.
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
# On Windows with PowerShell the line above is:  .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

# 3. The libraries we need, with their minimum version.
cat > requirements.txt <<'FIN'
psycopg[binary]>=3.2
pgvector>=0.3.6
numpy>=1.26
openai>=1.60
python-dotenv>=1.0
FIN

pip install -r requirements.txt

# 4. The key TEMPLATE. This file does get shared: it carries no secret.
cat > .env.example <<'FIN'
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres.abcdefgh:YOUR_PASSWORD@aws-0-eu-central-1.pooler.supabase.com:5432/postgres
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-proj-...
FIN

# 5. Your REAL key file, copied from the template.
cp .env.example .env

# 6. .gitignore: the list of what never leaves your computer.
#    If you push .env to GitHub, your key goes public and there are bots
#    crawling GitHub looking for exactly that. It gets spent within hours.
cat > .gitignore <<'FIN'
.env
.venv/
__pycache__/
FIN

# 7. Three documents from a made-up law firm, one per area.
cat > docs/general/vacaciones.md <<'FIN'
# Vacation policy

Each person at the firm gets 23 business days of vacation per year, plus the 2 personal days set by the collective agreement.

Vacation is requested in writing to your manager with 15 days' notice. In August the firm runs with half the staff, so that month only one request per team gets approved.

Unused days can be carried over to the next year until March 31st. After that date they are lost.
FIN

cat > docs/finanzas/gastos.md <<'FIN'
# Expense policy

Client meals are reimbursed up to €45 per person. Above that figure you need sign-off from the partner responsible for the matter.

Train travel is always booked in economy class. Preferente class on the Madrid-Barcelona AVE is only approved if the meeting starts before 10:00.

Receipts are submitted before the 5th of the following month. Anything that arrives later gets paid in the next month's payroll.
FIN

cat > docs/direccion/retribucion.md <<'FIN'
# 2026 salary bands

Junior lawyer, 0 to 3 years of practice: between €32,000 and €38,000 gross per year, spread over 14 payments.

Senior lawyer, 4 to 8 years: between €45,000 and €58,000 gross per year.

Partner: €70,000 fixed plus a variable of 8% on the billing of the matters they lead.

The salary review closes in January and is communicated by the managing partner in the annual review.
FIN

echo "Done. Now open .env and put in your two real keys."
steps.expected: At the end, a 'Done. Now open .env and put in your two real keys.' If you run ls docs/*/ you see the three .md files, one in each folder. And the terminal prompt has (.venv) in front, which is how you know the virtual environment is on.
steps.trouble: "python: command not found" or the Microsoft Store opens. On Windows try py -m venv .venv instead of python -m venv .venv. If that doesn't work either, Python isn't on the PATH: reinstall it from python.org, checking the "Add Python to PATH" box, which is unchecked by default and is mistake number one.

steps.title: Create the tables and the index in Postgres
steps.why: Vectors need to be stored somewhere that knows how to compare them fast. Plain Postgres doesn't know how; with the pgvector extension, it does. Here you create three tables: who's who, what documents exist, and what chunks they're split into. And the HNSW index, which is the difference between searching in 30 milliseconds or 4 seconds once you have 50,000 chunks.
steps.code:
-- esquema.sql
-- Paste it whole into Supabase's SQL Editor and click Run.

-- 1. pgvector: the extension that teaches Postgres to store and compare
--    vectors. Without this line, the "vector" type doesn't exist.
create extension if not exists vector;

-- 2. Who's who and which areas they belong to.
--    areas is an ARRAY of text: a person can be in several.
create table if not exists personas (
  email text primary key,
  areas text[] not null
);

-- 3. The documents. "area" is the folder the file came from,
--    and it's the only thing that decides who can read it.
create table if not exists documentos (
  id      bigserial primary key,
  ruta    text unique not null,
  titulo  text not null,
  area    text not null
);

-- 4. The chunks. Each one stores its text and its embedding: the list of
--    1536 numbers that represents its meaning.
--    on delete cascade: if you delete a document, its chunks go with it.
--    It's a real delete, no trash can.
create table if not exists trozos (
  id            bigserial primary key,
  documento_id  bigint not null references documentos(id) on delete cascade,
  orden         int not null,
  texto         text not null,
  embedding     vector(1536) not null
);

-- 5. The HNSW index. Without it, searching among 50,000 chunks compares
--    all 50,000 one by one. With it, it looks at a few hundred. From 4 seconds to 30 ms.
--    vector_cosine_ops = compare by angle, which is what OpenAI uses.
create index if not exists trozos_embedding_idx
  on trozos using hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);

create index if not exists trozos_documento_idx on trozos (documento_id);

-- 6. Three test people with different permissions.
insert into personas (email, areas) values
  ('ana@bufete.es',    array['general']),
  ('marcos@bufete.es', array['general','finanzas']),
  ('elena@bufete.es',  array['general','finanzas','direccion'])
on conflict (email) do update set areas = excluded.areas;
steps.expected: Supabase answers "Success. No rows returned". Go to Table Editor and you see the three new tables, and personas has 3 rows: ana, marcos, and elena. Save this SQL as esquema.sql inside the project folder even after running it: it's the recipe to rebuild it from scratch.
steps.trouble: "type \"vector\" does not exist". You ran only part of the block, without the first line. Select all the text and click Run again, starting from create extension if not exists vector.

steps.title: Connect Python to the database
steps.why: A single file that knows how to open the connection, and everything else calls it. If you move from Supabase to another server tomorrow, you change one line in .env and touch nothing else. This is also where the vector type gets activated on the connection: without that line, Python sends Postgres a list of numbers that Postgres doesn't understand.
steps.code:
# db.py
# A single place in the whole project that knows how to open the database.

import os
import psycopg
from psycopg.rows import dict_row
from pgvector.psycopg import register_vector
from dotenv import load_dotenv

# Reads the .env file and puts its lines into environment variables.
# The key is never written in the code: it's written in .env, which doesn't get pushed.
load_dotenv()

URL = os.environ.get("DATABASE_URL")
if not URL:
    raise SystemExit(
        "DATABASE_URL is missing. Open .env and paste in Supabase's "
        "connection string (Project Settings > Database > Connection string > URI)."
    )


def conectar():
    """Opens the connection, activates the vector type, and returns rows as dicts."""
    con = psycopg.connect(URL, row_factory=dict_row)
    register_vector(con)   # without this, psycopg doesn't know what a vector is
    return con


# Quick test: python db.py
if __name__ == "__main__":
    with conectar() as con, con.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute("select count(*) as n from personas")
        print("Connected. People on file:", cur.fetchone()["n"])
steps.expected: python db.py answers: Connected. People on file: 3. If it says 3, the connection string is right and the schema was created correctly. This is where most people get stuck; if you get past this, the rest goes smoothly.
steps.trouble: "password authentication failed" or it hangs without saying anything. It's almost always the password: Supabase's connection string has [YOUR-PASSWORD] in brackets and you have to replace that including the brackets. If your password has @, #, or /, those characters break the URL: change it in Supabase to letters and numbers only. And if it takes 30 seconds and dies, your Free project is paused: go to the dashboard and click Restore.

steps.title: Chunk the documents
steps.why: A model can't read an 80-page manual to answer a question, and even if it could, it would be very expensive and answer worse. You split it into chunks and only show it the 5 that are relevant. The trick is where you cut: by paragraph, not by character count, leaving 200 characters of overlap so a sentence split right at the cut still appears whole in some chunk.
steps.code:
# trocear.py
# Splits a long document into chunks that fit inside an answer.

def _partir_bloque(bloque: str, tam: int, solape: int) -> list[str]:
    """A lone paragraph longer than the limit has to be brute-force cut."""
    piezas, i = [], 0
    while i < len(bloque):
        piezas.append(bloque[i:i + tam])
        i += tam - solape
    return piezas


def trocear(texto: str, tam: int = 1200, solape: int = 200) -> list[str]:
    """
    tam    = 1200 characters, about 200 words. Not so much that the chunk
             mixes three topics, not so little that it cuts a sentence in half.
    solape = 200 characters repeated from the previous chunk. Ensures a
             sentence split at the cut still appears whole in some chunk.
    """
    parrafos = [p.strip() for p in texto.split("\n\n") if p.strip()]

    bloques = []
    for p in parrafos:
        bloques.extend(_partir_bloque(p, tam, solape) if len(p) > tam else [p])

    trozos, actual = [], ""
    for b in bloques:
        if not actual:
            actual = b
        elif len(actual) + len(b) + 2 <= tam:
            actual = actual + "\n\n" + b        # still fits, accumulate
        else:
            trozos.append(actual)               # close the chunk
            # Carry over the end of the previous one, but only if doing so
            # still lets the new chunk fit. If not, start clean.
            # Watch the "if solape": in Python, actual[-0:] returns the
            # WHOLE string, not an empty one. Without this check, setting
            # solape=0 to test would make chunks grow forever.
            cola = actual[-solape:] if solape and len(b) + solape + 2 <= tam else ""
            actual = (cola + "\n\n" + b).strip() if cola else b
    if actual:
        trozos.append(actual)
    return trozos


# Test: python trocear.py
if __name__ == "__main__":
    from pathlib import Path
    texto = Path("docs/general/vacaciones.md").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    for i, t in enumerate(trocear(texto)):
        print(f"--- chunk {i + 1} ({len(t)} characters) ---")
        print(t[:120].replace("\n", " "), "...")
steps.expected: python trocear.py prints the chunks from the vacation file. With such a short document you get just one, about 500 characters, and its first line is "# Vacation policy". To actually see it split, lower tam to 300 and run it again: you'll see 2 or 3 chunks and the end of one repeated at the start of the next. That's the overlap.
steps.trouble: "FileNotFoundError: docs/general/vacaciones.md". You're running from the wrong folder. Every command in this project is launched from inside buscador-docs, not from the folder above it. Check with pwd where you are.

steps.title: Index: turn each chunk into numbers and save it
steps.why: This is where text becomes searchable by meaning. Each chunk gets sent to OpenAI and comes back turned into 1536 numbers that represent what it's talking about. Two chunks that say the same thing in different words end up with similar numbers, and that's why "how much do I get paid for eating with a client" finds a text where none of those words appear.
steps.code:
# indexar.py
# Reads docs/, chunks it, turns each chunk into a vector, and saves it.

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
from openai import OpenAI

from db import conectar
from trocear import trocear

MODELO = "text-embedding-3-small"   # 1536 numbers per chunk
LOTE = 64                            # how many chunks per API call

cliente = OpenAI()   # picks up OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment, loaded by db.py


def titulo_de(texto: str, ruta: Path) -> str:
    """The file's first '# Heading'; if there isn't one, the file name."""
    for linea in texto.splitlines():
        if linea.startswith("# "):
            return linea[2:].strip()
    return ruta.stem.replace("-", " ").capitalize()


def vectorizar(textos: list[str]) -> list[list[float]]:
    respuesta = cliente.embeddings.create(model=MODELO, input=textos)
    return [d.embedding for d in respuesta.data]


def main():
    archivos = sorted(Path("docs").glob("*/*.md"))
    if not archivos:
        raise SystemExit("Nothing found under docs/<area>/*.md")

    total = 0
    with conectar() as con:
        for ruta in archivos:
            area = ruta.parent.name          # the folder IS the permission
            texto = ruta.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
            trozos = trocear(texto)

            with con.cursor() as cur:
                # Create/update the document record.
                cur.execute(
                    """
                    insert into documentos (ruta, titulo, area)
                    values (%s, %s, %s)
                    on conflict (ruta) do update
                      set titulo = excluded.titulo, area = excluded.area
                    returning id
                    """,
                    (ruta.as_posix(), titulo_de(texto, ruta), area),
                )
                doc_id = cur.fetchone()["id"]

                # CAREFUL: this deletes this document's old chunks.
                # That's what lets you reindex without duplicating, but
                # it's a permanent delete. No undo.
                cur.execute("delete from trozos where documento_id = %s", (doc_id,))

                vectores = []
                for i in range(0, len(trozos), LOTE):
                    vectores.extend(vectorizar(trozos[i:i + LOTE]))

                for orden, (t, v) in enumerate(zip(trozos, vectores)):
                    cur.execute(
                        "insert into trozos (documento_id, orden, texto, embedding)"
                        " values (%s, %s, %s, %s)",
                        (doc_id, orden, t, np.array(v)),
                    )

            con.commit()
            total += len(trozos)
            print(f"{ruta.as_posix():40s} {len(trozos):3d} chunks   area={area}")

    print(f"\nDone. {total} chunks indexed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
steps.expected:
Three lines, one per document, with the chunk count and area. Something like:
docs/direccion/retribucion.md   1 chunks   area=direccion
docs/finanzas/gastos.md         1 chunks   area=finanzas
docs/general/vacaciones.md      1 chunks   area=general
And at the end "Done. 3 chunks indexed.". You can run it as many times as you want: it deletes each document's old chunks before inserting the new ones, so nothing duplicates. Watch out: that delete is permanent, no trash can.
steps.trouble: "openai.RateLimitError: You exceeded your current quota". It's not that you're going fast, it's that you have $0 balance. The OpenAI API has no free plan: go to platform.openai.com/settings/organization/billing and load $5. If the error is "AuthenticationError", the key in .env is copied wrong, usually a trailing space or leftover quotes.

steps.title: Search with permissions baked into the query
steps.why: This is the step that separates a toy from something you can show off at a company. The temptation is to search for the top 5 chunks and then, in Python, remove the ones the person can't see. That's wrong for two reasons: if 4 of the 5 were from leadership, you're left with 1 and the answer comes out thin; and worse, you've brought confidential text into your program's memory that you shouldn't have read at all. The filter goes inside the SQL, before picking the winners. And along the way we add a similarity threshold, so a chunk that was only a little similar doesn't end up propping up an answer.
steps.code:
# buscar.py
# Retrieves the chunks most similar to a question, ALREADY filtered by permissions.

import numpy as np
from openai import OpenAI

from db import conectar

MODELO = "text-embedding-3-small"

# Similarity floor: below this the chunk is discarded outright.
# It's low on purpose. With this model, two unrelated texts sit around
# 0.10, and a good match usually falls between 0.30 and 0.55.
# 0.15 throws out the junk without risking throwing out a marginal hit.
# It's not a universal truth: raise it to 0.30 and you'll start losing
# correct answers. Measure it against your own documents before tuning it.
UMBRAL = 0.15

cliente = OpenAI()


def areas_de(con, email: str) -> list[str]:
    """What areas this person belongs to. If they're not on file, none."""
    with con.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute("select areas from personas where email = %s", (email,))
        fila = cur.fetchone()
    return fila["areas"] if fila else []


def buscar(email: str, pregunta: str, k: int = 5) -> list[dict]:
    v = np.array(
        cliente.embeddings.create(model=MODELO, input=[pregunta]).data[0].embedding
    )

    with conectar() as con:
        areas = areas_de(con, email)
        if not areas:
            return []   # unknown person: sees absolutely nothing

        with con.cursor() as cur:
            # ef_search: how many candidates the index looks at before deciding.
            # With a narrow filter you need to raise it or you'll fall short of results.
            cur.execute("set local hnsw.ef_search = 100")

            # THE KEY POINT OF THE PROJECT:
            # the "where d.area = any(%s)" goes INSIDE the query.
            # If you filtered in Python after the limit 5, two things would
            # go wrong: you'd end up with 1 result out of 5, and you'd have
            # already brought into memory text that person can't see.
            # House rule: every filter goes in the SQL, none in Python.
            cur.execute(
                """
                select d.titulo, d.ruta, d.area, t.orden, t.texto,
                       1 - (t.embedding <=> %s) as parecido
                from trozos t
                join documentos d on d.id = t.documento_id
                where d.area = any(%s)
                  and 1 - (t.embedding <=> %s) >= %s
                order by t.embedding <=> %s
                limit %s
                """,
                (v, areas, v, UMBRAL, v, k),
            )
            return cur.fetchall()


# Test: python buscar.py
if __name__ == "__main__":
    for fila in buscar("marcos@bufete.es", "¿cuánto me pagan de una comida con cliente?"):
        print(f"{fila['parecido']:.0%}  {fila['titulo']}  [{fila['area']}]")
steps.expected: python buscar.py prints one line pointing to "Expense policy [finanzas]", with a similarity in the 40-60% range. Marcos is in finanzas, so he sees it. The percentages rarely go above 70% even when the result is perfect: it's not a score out of 100, it's how close two directions are in space. What matters is the order, not the figure.
steps.trouble: Returns an empty list. Three suspects, in this order: the email isn't written the same as in the personas table (marcos@bufete.es, not Marcos@bufete.es); indexing didn't finish (in Supabase, select count(*) from trozos has to give 3); or UMBRAL is too high for your documents. To find out which, temporarily lower UMBRAL to 0.0: if results show up then, it was the threshold.

steps.title: Answer while citing the source
steps.why: A search engine that spits out a nice paragraph without saying where it came from is no good at a company: nobody can verify it. Here the model receives the numbered chunks and has three orders: use only that, put the [1] or [2] marker after each fact, and say it can't find it if it isn't there. Temperature at 0 is what turns off creativity, which here is exactly what you don't want.
steps.code:
# responder.py
# Combines what was retrieved, hands it to the model, and returns the answer with sources.
#
# Usage:  python responder.py ana@bufete.es "¿cuántos días de vacaciones tengo?"

import sys

from openai import OpenAI

from buscar import buscar

MODELO = "gpt-4o-mini"
NO_SE = "I can't find that in the documents you have access to."

cliente = OpenAI()

INSTRUCCIONES = f"""You are a law firm's internal search assistant.

Rules, no exceptions:
- Answer ONLY with what's in the material. No outside knowledge.
- Put a marker after each fact: [1], [2]... matching the fragment number.
- If the material doesn't answer the question, write exactly: {NO_SE}
- Don't make up figures, dates, or names. If a figure isn't there, it isn't there.
- Answer in Spanish, under 120 words."""


def responder(email: str, pregunta: str):
    trozos = buscar(email, pregunta)
    if not trozos:
        return NO_SE, []

    material = "\n\n".join(
        f"[{i + 1}] {t['titulo']}, fragment {t['orden'] + 1}\n{t['texto']}"
        for i, t in enumerate(trozos)
    )

    r = cliente.chat.completions.create(
        model=MODELO,
        temperature=0,   # 0 = the least creative answer possible, which is what we want
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": INSTRUCCIONES},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"Material:\n{material}\n\nQuestion: {pregunta}"},
        ],
    )
    return r.choices[0].message.content.strip(), trozos


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 3:
        raise SystemExit('Usage: python responder.py email@firm.com "your question"')

    email, pregunta = sys.argv[1], " ".join(sys.argv[2:])
    texto, trozos = responder(email, pregunta)

    print(f"\n{texto}\n")
    if trozos:
        print("Sources:")
        for i, t in enumerate(trozos):
            print(f"  [{i + 1}] {t['titulo']} — {t['ruta']} "
                  f"(fragment {t['orden'] + 1}, similarity {t['parecido']:.0%})")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
steps.expected: python responder.py elena@bufete.es "¿cuánto cobra un abogado junior?" returns something like: "A junior lawyer, 0 to 3 years of practice, earns between €32,000 and €38,000 gross per year over 14 payments [1]." And below, the Sources list with the file docs/direccion/retribucion.md and its percentage. If a figure shows up that isn't in your document, something's wrong: check the material is being assembled correctly.
steps.trouble: Answers correctly but without the [1] markers. Usually happens when the question is very general and the model leans toward summarizing. Tighten the instructions: add "An answer without [n] markers is an invalid answer." to the end of the INSTRUCCIONES block. If the error is "model not found", your account doesn't have access to that model yet: change MODELO to gpt-4o-mini or whatever shows up for you at platform.openai.com/docs/models.

steps.title: Try to make it snitch, and confirm it doesn't
steps.why: Working with your own user proves nothing. What proves the project is serious is asking the same question with three different permission sets and getting three different answers. This test is what you show off in an interview, and the one you repeat every time you touch the search code, because a permissions leak doesn't throw an error: it gives a correct answer to someone who shouldn't have gotten it.
steps.code:
# Same question, three different people. This is the project's proof.

# Ana is only in 'general'. The salary band lives in 'direccion'.
python responder.py ana@bufete.es "¿cuánto cobra un abogado junior?"

# Elena is also in 'direccion'. She does see it.
python responder.py elena@bufete.es "¿cuánto cobra un abogado junior?"

# Ana isn't in 'finanzas' either: the meal cap doesn't reach her.
python responder.py ana@bufete.es "¿cuánto puedo gastar en una comida con cliente?"

# Marcos is in finanzas.
python responder.py marcos@bufete.es "¿cuánto puedo gastar en una comida con cliente?"

# Everyone sees 'general'.
python responder.py ana@bufete.es "¿cuántos días de vacaciones tengo?"

# Someone not on file sees NOTHING, not even the public stuff.
python responder.py intruso@gmail.com "¿cuántos días de vacaciones tengo?"
steps.expected:
Six answers. Elena gets the salary band, Marcos gets the €45 per person, and Ana gets her 23 vacation days with its source. The intruder gets nothing, not even the public information, because they're not in the personas table.

On the two questions Ana shouldn't be able to answer, you'll see "I can't find that in the documents you have access to." Tell two things apart, because they're not equally solid. That Ana NEVER gets the leadership text is guaranteed by the where in step 6: it's mechanical, it doesn't depend on anyone. That the refusal sentence also comes out exactly right is decided by the model, and a model can have an off day. extend: Reindex only what changed. Right now indexar.py revectorizes all three documents even if you haven't touched any. Store a hash column in the documentos table with the result of hashlib.sha256(texto.encode()).hexdigest(), and when starting each file, compare: if the hash is the same, skip it. With three documents it doesn't matter; with 4,000 it's the difference between a 6-second wait and a 20-minute one, and between a small bill and a big one.

Add hybrid search. Embeddings understand meaning but stumble on exact codes: if someone searches "case 2026-0483", the vector won't find it. Add a tsvector column with Postgres's classic text search, run both searches, and merge the results by summing 1/(60+position) from each list. That trick is called Reciprocal Rank Fusion and it's what real search engines use.

Switch from folder-level permissions to per-document, per-person permissions, and move them into Postgres Row Level Security. That's real security: the rules live in the database, not in your code, so even if someone writes a new query and forgets the filter, Postgres won't let them see what isn't theirs. It takes an afternoon to get your head around it, and it's what sets you apart from most candidates.
defend: "Why pgvector and not a dedicated vector database like Pinecone or Qdrant?" Because the permissions live in the same tables as the documents. With pgvector, filtering by area and sorting by similarity is a single query with a join, and Postgres guarantees only the right person sees it. With a separate vector database, you have the vectors in one place and the permissions in another, and you have to sync the two by hand: the day someone changes teams and the sync fails, you have a leak. At 50 million vectors with tight latency requirements, the answer changes and a dedicated database wins. Below a few million, Postgres has plenty of headroom and you save yourself an entire system.

"How do you know it doesn't make up the answers?" Three things, all verifiable. One, the model only receives the retrieved chunks, it has no other source. Two, temperature is at 0 and the instructions force it to put the fragment marker after each fact, so anyone can open the file and verify it in ten seconds. And three, it has an explicit fallback: if the material doesn't answer, it says it can't find it. That's not a mathematical guarantee, and I don't sell it as one: a model can cite wrong. That's why the answer always comes with the file path, so the final check is done by a person.

"Why not apply the permission filter after searching instead?" Because it fails two ways. The first is a quality problem: if you ask for the top 5 and 4 were from a forbidden area, you're left with 1 and the answer comes out thin, with nobody knowing why. The second is a security problem: to discard them you've had to pull them into memory, and from there all it takes is a stray log line or a verbose error message for that text to leave the system. The filter goes in the where, before picking the winners, so the forbidden text never leaves Postgres at all. And the next step, if this grows, is Row Level Security, so the rule doesn't even depend on me remembering to write the where.
